paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few medical advances have saved as many lives as vaccination. Smallpox, a disease that killed hundreds of millions of people in the twentieth century alone, was declared eradicated in 1980, the result of a worldwide vaccination campaign. Polio, once a cause of paralysis in children around the world, has been reduced by more than ninety-nine per cent since 1988. Yet the science behind these successes is not always well understood, and many people are unsure what a vaccine actually does inside the body.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To understand how a vaccine works, it helps to know how the immune system responds to infection. When a virus or bacterium enters the body, white blood cells recognise it as foreign by identifying molecules on its surface, known as antigens. Some of these cells produce antibodies, proteins that attach to the invader and mark it for destruction. The first time the body meets a new germ, this response takes several days, and during that time the person may become ill.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: After the infection, the immune system keeps memory cells, which can recognise the same germ if it returns and respond within hours rather than days. A vaccine exploits this memory. It contains a harmless version of the germ, such as a weakened or inactivated form, or just a piece of it, which trains the immune system without causing the disease. Some modern vaccines use instructions in the form of genetic material that tell cells to make a single antigen, so that the body can learn to recognise it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all vaccines last for life. Measles vaccination, given in two doses, provides protection for decades, whereas the influenza vaccine must be renewed each year, because the virus changes constantly. Scientists predict which strains will be common and design the vaccine months in advance, so its effectiveness varies from year to year, typically between forty and sixty per cent.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Vaccines also protect people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or those with weak immune systems. This effect, called herd immunity, occurs when enough of a population is immune that the disease cannot spread easily. For highly infectious diseases such as measles, around ninety-five per cent of people need to be vaccinated to achieve it. When coverage falls below that level, outbreaks can occur, as they have in several countries in recent years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Like all medicines, vaccines can cause side effects, which are usually mild, such as a sore arm or a brief fever. Serious reactions are extremely rare, and extensive monitoring systems exist to detect them. Weighing the risks and benefits, health authorities conclude that for approved vaccines, the benefits far exceed the risks. Understanding how they work is one of the best ways to counter the misinformation that spreads so easily today.
